key_terms.meaning: An organised system of hardware, software, data, people and methods that captures, stores, queries, analyses and displays spatially referenced data to answer questions.
Five parts: hardware, software, data, people, and methods (procedures); data is usually the most costly part.
The where: coordinates and geometry that fix a feature's position on the earth.
The what: non-location facts about a feature stored in a table and joined to geometry by a key.
Names or labels with no order, e.g. land-use class = residential, paddy field, tank.
Ranked labels where order matters but gaps are unknown, e.g. road class = village, district, national highway.
Numbers with equal intervals but an arbitrary zero, e.g. temperature in °C.
Numbers with equal intervals and a true zero, so ratios mean something, e.g. distance 4 km is twice 2 km.
Ground features stored as points (x, y), lines (strings of x, y) and polygons (closed lines), each with an attribute record.
Space divided into a grid of square cells, each cell holding one value such as elevation in metres or a land-use code.; storage = rows × columns × bits per cell ÷ 8
One raster square; its size (say 5 m × 5 m) fixes the smallest detail the raster can show.
Converting a paper map or an image into vector or raster data by tracing, scanning or on-screen clicking with control points.
Checking edited data against independent evidence, e.g. total station coordinates or field notes, before analysis.
RMS = √((Σe<sub>i</sub>² + Σn<sub>i</sub>²) ÷ n) over n control points; compare with 0.25 mm × scale
The reference surface and constants (ellipsoid plus its position) on which coordinates are computed, e.g. WGS84.
A set of equations that maps latitude and longitude on the curved earth onto a flat x, y plane, always with some distortion.
World Geodetic System 1984: the global datum of GPS/GNSS positions, giving latitude, longitude and ellipsoidal height.
Universal Transverse Mercator: a set of 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, giving coordinates in metres on a transverse Mercator projection.
zone = floor((longitude + 180) ÷ 6) + 1; central meridian scale factor 0.9996, false easting 500 000 m
Combining two or more layers of the same area to produce a new layer that carries attributes of both.
A zone drawn at a fixed distance d around a feature, e.g. 200 m either side of a river for a protected margin.
Replacing cell or polygon values with new classes, e.g. slope 0–5 % → class 1, so layers become comparable.
S = Σ w<sub>i</sub> s<sub>i</sub> with Σ w<sub>i</sub> = 1
slope = arctan √((∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)²); aspect = atan2(−∂z/∂x, −∂z/∂y), from 0° to 360°

takeaways: A GIS answers questions about places; drawing a map is only its output, not its purpose.
Every feature carries location and attributes joined by a key, so the table and the geometry must stay consistent.
Raster wins on continuous surfaces and fast computation; vector wins on precise boundaries and compact storage.
Most of the effort in a real GIS project goes into input, editing and verification, not into analysis.
Layers in different datums or projections will not line up, so every layer must carry its datum, projection and units.
Overlay, proximity and reclassification turn single layers into answers that no one layer can give.
Drought, flood and facility-planning studies show the value of GIS best, because they need several layers ranked together.
A wrong attribute in a clean geometry gives a confident wrong answer, so verify both position and value.
bank_note: Most syllabi want the definition and five components, the raster–vector comparison, the input-to-analysis pipeline, and one applied case such as drought management or facility planning, so prepare a full worked example with layers named.

bank.q: Define GIS and describe its five components. State one function of each with an Indian example.
outline: Definition stresses organised system for spatially referenced data and question answering, not just map drawing
Hardware: computers, plotters, GNSS receivers, drones
Software: QGIS or similar for capture, storage, analysis, display
Data: spatial + attribute; the costliest component
People: surveyors, analysts, decision makers
Methods: standards, procedures, quality checks
Example: a municipal corporation using one system for property tax, water lines and ward boundaries

answer.text: Definition. A GIS is an organised system of hardware, software, data, people and methods that captures, stores, manages, analyses and displays spatially referenced data in order to answer questions about places. The analysis, combining layers through location, is what separates it from a map-drawing program.
The five components, each with one function and an Indian example:

head: Component
Function
Example
rows: capture and output: computers, servers, GNSS receivers, scanners, plotters, drones
a municipal office with a server, field tablets and a plotter
the layers and their attribute tables; usually the costliest part
ward boundaries, property parcels, water mains
surveyors capture, analysts query, engineers decide
the corporation's GIS cell and its engineers
written rules: datum, projection, scale, accuracy, update cycle
a rule that all layers use WGS84 and UTM zone 44

answer.text: The four functions that run through the components: input, storage and management, manipulation and analysis, output.

Worked illustration. A corporation lists streets within 200 m of a new metro station that have no water main. The software buffers the station (area π × 200² = 125 664 m²), selects four streets inside, drops the two with mains, and reports Market Street and Lake Road: 2√(200² − 80²) + 2√(200² − 190²) = 366.6 + 124.9 = 491.5 m of new pipe. Data supplied the layers, methods ensured they share one projection, people chose the route.
Why the components matter: drop people or methods and the layers drift out of date or out of alignment; drop the data and the software has nothing to analyse.

Data in more detail: spatial data (the geometry, as points, lines, polygons or a grid of cells) and attribute data (the table of properties), joined through a key field. A water-main layer stores each pipe as a line with diameter, material and year laid, so a query such as "mains older than 30 years inside the buffer" uses both halves at once.

Methods in more detail: a city layer captured at 1:4000 is allowed 0.25 mm × 4000 = 1.0 m of error, while a 1:50 000 layer is allowed 0.25 mm × 50 000 = 12.5 m. A written method says which scale may be used for which decision, so a pipe is never laid out from a district-scale sheet.

bank.q: Distinguish spatial data from attribute data. Explain how the two are linked, and describe the four measurement scales with one surveying example each.
outline: Spatial = where, stored as coordinates and geometry
Attribute = what, stored as a table row
Link through a common key field such as plot number
Nominal: named classes, land-use type
Ordinal: ranked, road hierarchy
Interval: equal intervals, arbitrary zero, e.g. temperature in °C or a reduced level on an assumed benchmark
Ratio: true zero, distance, area, discharge
Why it matters: only ratio and interval data allow arithmetic; nominal data allows only counting

answer.text: Spatial data is the "where": coordinates in a stated system (easting and northing in metres), plus shape, size, orientation and stored topology. A well is a point, a pipe a line, a parcel a polygon.
Attribute data is the "what": a table in which each row is a feature and each column a property, such as type, depth or owner.

Link. A key field with a unique value per feature (well number, survey number, plot number) joins each attribute row to its geometry. A join to another table, such as wards, uses a shared key of the same type: text '07' does not match number 7 until one side is converted.
The four measurement scales, with surveying examples:

head: Scale
Property
Surveying example
Valid operations
rows: road class (village, district, national highway); condition rank 1–5
reduced level on an assumed benchmark (RL 100.000); temperature in °C

answer.text: Worked case. Four wells: depths 40, 55, 80, 65 m (ratio), types open, open, bore, bore (nominal). The attribute query depth > 60 m returns wells 3 and 4. The spatial query "inside ward 7", with ward 7 the area 400 ≤ E ≤ 416 m, tests the eastings 412, 415, 418, 421 m and returns wells 1 and 2. Mean depth = (40 + 55 + 80 + 65) ÷ 4 = 60 m is meaningful; a "mean ward" (7 + 7 + 9 + 9) ÷ 4 = 8 is not, because ward is a nominal label.

Why it matters. The scale decides which arithmetic the GIS may apply: averaging a nominal code or taking a ratio of interval values (an RL of 200 m is not "twice as high" as one of 100 m on an assumed datum) gives numbers with no meaning.
Check. 40 + 55 + 80 + 65 = 240, and 240 ÷ 4 = 60 m; the depth query and the ward query select different wells because they test different halves of the record.

bank.q: Compare the raster and vector data models under storage, precision, analysis speed and suitability, and state where each is preferred.
outline: Raster: grid of cells, one value per cell, cell size sets resolution
Vector: points, lines, polygons with coordinates plus attribute records
Storage: raster grows with area/cell size squared; vector compact for simple features
Precision: vector boundaries exact; raster boundaries stepped
Analysis: raster fast for continuous surfaces and map algebra; vector better for networks and boundaries
Topology and network analysis natural in vector
Examples: elevation, rainfall, land cover as raster; cadastral parcels, pipelines, roads as vector
Conversion is possible both ways with loss

answer.text: Vector model: points (x, y), lines (ordered vertices) and polygons (closed rings), each with an attribute record; topology records which lines meet and which polygons share an edge.
Raster model: a grid of square cells with an origin, a cell size, rows and columns, and one value per cell (elevation, class code or image band).

Storage, with numbers. A 10 km pipeline with a vertex every 10 m needs 1001 vertices × 16 bytes = 16 016 bytes (16 kB) as a vector. A 5 m raster of the 10 km × 10 km area needs 2000 × 2000 cells × 1 byte = 4 000 000 bytes (4 MB), 250 times more, because every empty cell is stored. Raster storage grows with (area ÷ cell size²): halving the cell size multiplies it by 4.

Precision. A vector boundary is as exact as its surveyed coordinates. A raster boundary follows whole cells: with 20 m cells a boundary can be up to 10 m (half a cell) from its true line, and an area is counted in 400 m² steps: on a 3 × 4 grid of 20 m cells, the four cells at or above 35 m give exactly 4 × 400 = 1600 m², whatever the true contour encloses.

Analysis speed and type. Raster overlay is cell by cell, so map algebra (slope, suitability, flood depth) is simple and fast. Vector overlay must intersect lines and rebuild topology, which is heavier, but buffers, network tracing and shortest paths are natural in vector.
Comparison:

Where each is preferred: vector for cadastral parcels, pipelines, roads, wells and any network; raster for elevation, rainfall, land cover and remote sensing images. Many projects keep both, vector pipes over a raster DEM.
Conversion. Rasterising draws lines into cells and loses exact position; vectorising traces cell edges and produces stepped or smoothed lines. Both lose detail at the cell size.
Check. 16 016 × 250 = 4 004 000 ≈ 4 000 000 bytes; 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m maximum boundary error.

bank.q: Explain datum, projection and coordinate system. Why must every GIS layer record all three and its units?
outline: Datum: ellipsoid plus its placement, defines the reference frame, e.g. WGS84
Projection: equations mapping latitude/longitude to flat x, y, with unavoidable distortion of shape, area, distance or direction
Coordinate system: the numbered plane, e.g. UTM easting/northing in metres within a named zone
Same point can have different numbers under different datums, a shift of a hundred metres or more between some older Indian and global frames
Mismatched layers produce apparent offsets that look like digitising errors
Best practice: store datum, projection, units and zone as layer metadata; reproject before overlay

answer.text: Datum. A reference ellipsoid (a smooth mathematical surface close to the earth) fixed to the earth with a stated origin and orientation, so latitude and longitude name one place. WGS84 is the global GNSS datum; older Indian sheets use the Everest ellipsoid with an older Indian datum.

Projection. Equations that turn latitude and longitude on the curved ellipsoid into x and y on a plane. No projection keeps shape, area, distance and direction all at once; transverse Mercator (used by UTM) keeps shape.

Coordinate system. The numbered plane that results, with origin, axes and units, such as UTM zone 44 N in metres: zone = floor((80 + 180) ÷ 6) + 1 = 44 for a point at 80° E; central meridian 81° E; scale factor 0.9996 there; false easting 500 000 m.
Units. Degrees and metres are not interchangeable: 1° of longitude is about 111 km at the equator but 111.3 × cos 13° = 108.4 km near Chennai, so geometry in degrees is distorted.

What goes wrong without them. A layer on a different datum sits a hundred metres or more off; at 1:50 000 the allowed error is only 0.25 mm × 50 000 = 12.5 m, so the shift is ten times the tolerance and looks like a digitising error. A layer in degrees loaded as metres lands near the origin of the grid; a missing zone puts features 6° (about 650 km) away.

Best practice: record datum, projection, zone and units in each layer's metadata (a registry code such as EPSG:32644 says WGS84 / UTM zone 44N in one number), reproject layers to one system before overlay, and transform datums with stated parameters, because on-the-fly reprojection fixes the projection only.

Worked conversion. A point at 80° E, 13° N lies 1° west of the central meridian, about 108.4 km on the ground. Multiplied by 0.9996 and subtracted from the false easting, it gives an easting of roughly 500 000 − 108 400 = 391 600 m, with the northing measured from the equator (about 1 437 km). The same point read in degrees on another layer would be (80, 13), nowhere near (391 600, 1 437 000), which is why the units must be stated.
Check. Zone 44 covers 78° to 84° E, so 80° E is inside it; 0.9996 × 1000 = 999.6 m on the grid for a 1000 m ellipsoid distance at the central meridian.

bank.q: A district wants to site a new higher secondary school for rural habitations. Describe, layer by layer, how you would use buffer, overlay and reclassification, and what output map you would give.
outline: Layer 1: settlement points with population attribute
Layer 2: existing schools, buffered at a chosen service radius, say 5 km
Layer 3: road network, buffered, or walkable distance surface
Layer 4: unsuitable land: water bodies, steep slope, reserved forest
Reclassify each layer to a common 1–5 suitability score
Overlay by weighted sum or intersection to get candidate polygons
Query polygons outside existing buffers, on suitable land, adjacent to road
Field verification of shortlisted sites, then rank by population served
State the assumptions and the data scale openly

answer.text: Goal and output: a ranked map of candidate sites for a higher secondary school that serves rural habitations now more than 5 km from any such school.

Layer 1, habitations (points) with child population; layer 2, existing higher secondary schools (points); layer 3, roads (lines); layer 4, unsuitable land: tanks and rivers, reserved forest, slopes above 15 percent (polygons and a DEM-derived raster). All layers are put in one datum and projection first.

Buffer existing schools at 5 km: each buffer covers π × 5² = 78.5 km². Habitations outside every buffer are the unserved ones (a spatial query). Buffer roads at 500 m, because a school must be reachable by bus.
Reclassify each factor to a common 1–5 score with stated breaks:

Weighted overlay: S = Σ w<sub>i</sub> s<sub>i</sub> with Σ w<sub>i</sub> = 1. With weights 0.6 for children and 0.4 for distance from existing schools, three candidate villages score: A (5, 2): 0.6 × 5 + 0.4 × 2 = 3.8; B (4, 4): 2.4 + 1.6 = 4.0; C (2, 5): 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.2. B ranks first although A has more children, because A is already fairly close to a school.
Constraint overlay: erase (or score 0) all land in layer 4 and outside the road buffer, so no candidate sits in a tank or on a steep slope.
Catchment check: a 2 km buffer round the chosen site covers π × 2000² = 12.57 km², 13 963 cells of 30 m; sum the children inside it from the habitation layer to report the population served.

Output: a suitability map in five classes, a table of the top sites with S, children served and distance to road, and a note of data dates and scales. Field-verify the top three sites (land title, access, flooding) before the final choice.
Check. 0.6 + 0.4 = 1.0, so S stays on the 1–5 scale; 3.8 < 4.0 > 3.2, B is best; 78.5 km² = π × 25.

bank.q: Describe the steps to convert a paper cadastral map into a clean vector layer in a GIS, including the checks you would run.
outline: Scan at adequate resolution, note the map projection and scale
Choose enough control points spread over the sheet; record their coordinates by total station or GNSS
Georeference with an affine or polynomial transform; report residual error in metres
On-screen digitise points, lines, polygons; set snapping and topology rules
Attach attribute fields: survey number, owner, area, land-use code
Edit errors: undershoots, overshoots, dangling nodes, duplicate lines, slivers
Check polygon closure and compare computed area with record area
Verify a random sample against field measurement before accepting the layer

answer.text: Scan the sheet at a resolution fine enough for the map's line work (for a 1:4000 village map, 0.1 mm on the paper is 0.4 m on the ground); note the sheet's scale, projection and any grid printed on it.
Control points: choose at least four, spread to the corners and middle, whose ground coordinates are known (survey stones fixed by total station or GNSS, or printed grid intersections).

Georeference: fit an affine transformation (three points fix it exactly; four or more give residuals) or a second-order fit for a warped sheet (six or more points). Report the residuals and the RMS error.
Accept or refit: the 1:4000 tolerance is 0.25 mm × 4000 = 1.0 m; 0.45 m is inside it, and no single residual exceeds √(0.4² + 0.2²) = 0.45 m, so the fit is accepted.
Digitise on screen with snapping on, so neighbouring parcels share one boundary line; build parcels as polygons and survey stones as points.
Attributes: survey number (the key, unique), owner, record area, land-use code from a fixed list (a domain), each field with its type.

Edit and topology: remove duplicate nodes, extend undershoots and trim overshoots (both leave dangles), close open polygons, delete slivers, then build topology and confirm no dangles, gaps or overlaps remain.

Checks: compare each digitised area with the record. Parcel 112: record 0.8400 ha, digitised 0.8312 ha, difference (0.8312 − 0.8400) ÷ 0.8400 = −1.05 %, inside a ±2 % acceptance band. Count parcels against the sheet (completeness), edge-match with neighbouring sheets, and field-check a random sample of boundaries and owners; report attribute accuracy with the sample size (for example 46 of 50 correct, 92 %).
Record metadata: source sheet, scan date, control points, RMS 0.45 m, datum and projection, and the checks run.

Reading the residuals: a sheet that has shrunk unevenly in storage shows large residuals that all point one way along one edge; extra control points there or a second-order fit removes them. A single bad control point shows one large residual among small ones, and is re-measured or dropped before the fit is accepted.

bank.q: Explain how GIS layers of rainfall, soil moisture, crop condition and irrigation coverage are combined to map drought risk in a district.
outline: Define the drought indicator first, e.g. rainfall departure from normal as a percentage
Reclassify each layer to common severity classes 1–4
Assign weights reflecting local judgement; normalise weights to sum to one
Overlay by weighted sum to get a drought severity index per polygon or pixel
Validate against reported crop loss or ground truth from sample villages
Output maps of vulnerable villages for relief planning and tanker routing
Note the difference between meteorological, hydrological and agricultural drought

answer.text: Define the indicators first: rainfall departure from normal, D = (actual − normal) ÷ normal × 100 percent; soil moisture from a field or satellite product; crop condition from the NDVI anomaly against the same week in normal years; irrigation coverage as the fraction of cropped area irrigated.
Put all layers on one grid or one set of village polygons, one datum and one season, and use zonal statistics to get one value per village.
Reclassify each to severity classes 1 (low) to 4 (severe) with stated breaks; irrigation is reversed, since more irrigation lowers risk:
Weights by local judgement, normalised to 1: rainfall 0.40, soil moisture 0.25, crop condition 0.25, irrigation 0.10.

Village X: normal 800 mm, actual 460 mm: D = (460 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = −42.5 %, class 4; soil moisture 35 %, class 3; NDVI anomaly −0.15, class 3; irrigated 15 %, class 4. Index = 0.40 × 4 + 0.25 × 3 + 0.25 × 3 + 0.10 × 4 = 1.60 + 0.75 + 0.75 + 0.40 = 3.50.
Village Y: normal 800 mm, actual 680 mm: D = −15 %, class 2; soil moisture 50 %, class 2; NDVI anomaly −0.04, class 1; irrigated 55 %, class 2. Index = 0.80 + 0.50 + 0.25 + 0.20 = 1.75.
Map the index in four classes; X (3.50) is severe and goes on the relief list, Y (1.75) is mild. Validate against reported crop loss in sample villages before release.

Note the drought types: meteorological (rainfall shortage, the D layer), agricultural (soil moisture and crop stress), hydrological (low reservoirs and groundwater, a further layer if available). The weights decide which type the map emphasises.
Output: a village-level drought severity map and a ranked list for relief, fodder and tanker routing, with data dates stated.
Check. 0.40 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.10 = 1.00, so the index stays between 1 and 4; −340 ÷ 800 = −0.425.

bank.q: How would you combine a UAV orthomosaic, a GNSS survey and a LiDAR point cloud into one GIS for monitoring a highway construction site?
outline: Set one datum, projection and unit for the whole project, e.g. WGS84 and a UTM zone in metres
GNSS provides ground control points that anchor both UAV and LiDAR data
UAV RGB images processed by structure-from-motion to give orthomosaic and a surface model
LiDAR gives dense elevation and vegetation or stockpile volumes
Reconcile vertical datums and remove systematic offsets using checkpoints
Store as separate layers with metadata; compute cut-fill from DEM differences between epochs
Report positional and vertical accuracy explicitly
Use the same layers to check progress against the design alignment

answer.text: One reference frame first: WGS84 with UTM zone 44 N in metres for plan, and one vertical datum. GNSS gives ellipsoidal heights h; the design uses orthometric heights H = h − N, where N is the geoid undulation from a geoid model. With N = −86.5 m at the site (given), a GNSS height of h = 12.3 m is H = 12.3 + 86.5 = 98.8 m. Mixing h and H puts the surfaces 86.5 m apart.
GNSS survey: ground control points (GCPs) and independent check points along the corridor, fixed by RTK or static GNSS; they anchor both the drone and the LiDAR data.

UAV: plan the flight for the ground sample distance GSD = pixel size × flying height ÷ focal length. With 2.4 µm pixels, an 8.8 mm lens and 100 m height, GSD = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 ÷ 8.8 × 10⁻³ = 0.027 m, 2.7 cm. Process the overlapping photos by structure from motion into an orthomosaic and a surface model, tied to the GCPs.
LiDAR: a classified point cloud; ground points give a bare-earth DEM, and other classes give stockpiles, vegetation and structures.

Reconcile: compare each product at the check points; remove any constant vertical offset; report RMSE. Example: check-point differences of +0.03, −0.02, +0.04, −0.01 m give RMSE = √((0.0009 + 0.0004 + 0.0016 + 0.0001) ÷ 4) = √0.00075 = 0.027 m.
Store as layers with metadata: design alignment (vector), GCPs (points), orthomosaics by date (raster), DEMs by date (raster), and progress notes (attributes).

Cut and fill from DEM differences: subtract the earlier DEM from the later one cell by cell. On a 0.5 m grid, a stockpile covering 2400 cells with a mean rise of 1.8 m holds 2400 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.8 = 1080 m³.
Monitoring uses: compare the built formation with the design levels, track earthwork quantities for payment, find encroachments on the right of way, and record each epoch with its accuracy.

bank.q: For a water supply network and for a terrain slope map, choose raster or vector and justify each choice on storage, precision and analysis.
outline: Network: vector, for topological connectivity, pipe attributes, tracing and shortest path
Network precision: pipe junctions fixed by coordinates, not cells
Terrain slope: raster, for continuous surface, map algebra, fast computation
Slope from a DEM by neighbourhood operation on cells
Storage trade-off with cell size
Possible hybrid: vector pipes over a raster base map
State that conversion between models loses detail

answer.text: Water supply network: vector. Pipes are lines and valves, hydrants and junctions are points; topology records which pipe joins which node, so the GIS can trace flow, isolate a section by closing valves and find the shortest path.
Storage for the network: 120 km of pipe with a vertex every 20 m is 6000 vertices × 16 bytes = 96 000 bytes, about 96 kB, plus the attribute table (diameter, material, year).

Precision for the network: junctions and valves are fixed by surveyed coordinates to centimetres; a raster of 1 m cells would place them only to within the cell and would need 10⁸ cells for a 10 km × 10 km town.
Terrain slope: raster. Elevation varies continuously, so a DEM grid holds a value everywhere, and slope is a focal (3 × 3 neighbourhood) operation done the same way for every cell.

Slope with numbers: for a 30 m DEM cell with neighbours east 104, west 96, north 110, south 98 m, ∂z/∂x = 8 ÷ 60 = 0.133 and ∂z/∂y = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.200, so slope = arctan √(0.133² + 0.200²) = arctan 0.240 = 13.5° (24.0 %), aspect 213.7°.

Storage for the slope map: a 10 km × 10 km DEM at 10 m is 1000 × 1000 cells × 4 bytes = 4 MB; at 5 m it is 16 MB. Halving the cell quadruples storage, so pick the cell size from the slope detail needed.
Hybrid: draw the vector network over the raster slope map, for example to find pipes on slopes above 15 percent.
Converting either model to the other loses detail at the cell size, so keep each in its natural model.

Different questions, different operations: the vector network answers "which customers lose supply if valve V12 is closed?" by tracing the pipes downstream of V12, while the raster answers "what is the slope at every cell?" by neighbourhood map algebra. Each data set stays in the model whose operations it needs.

Accuracy note: a 30 m DEM cannot show a 2 m embankment, so a pipe crossing one needs field levels or a 1 m LiDAR DEM; the cell size limits the slope detail just as the vertex spacing limits the pipe detail.

bank.q: Two layers of the same area do not line up in an overlay. Analyse the possible causes and state how you would test and correct each.
outline: Different datums: a constant shift of a hundred metres or more; test by comparing common control points
Different projections or missing projection information; reproject to a common system
Different units, degrees versus metres
Digitising errors and residual georeferencing error from too few control points
Mixed scales of source maps
Generalisation differences causing sliver polygons along shared boundaries
Test: overlay known identical features such as road junctions and measure offsets
Correct: reproject, re-georeference, snap and clean topology, then recheck

answer.text: Measure first. Pick features that must coincide in both layers (road junctions, bridge ends, survey stones) and record the offset ΔE, ΔN at each. The pattern of offsets points to the cause.

Cause 1, different datums. Offsets are nearly the same everywhere, a hundred metres or more. Example: (+152, +214), (+150, +216), (+153, +213) m at three junctions: a constant shift of about 262 m (√(152² + 214²) = 262.5). Test: read both layers' metadata; correct by a datum transformation with stated parameters, not by moving the layer by eye.

Cause 2, different or missing projection. Offsets grow or turn across the area, or one layer is in degrees. Test: check the projection and zone; correct by reprojecting to the common system. A missing zone can place a layer 6° (about 650 km) away.

Cause 3, wrong units. Offsets grow in proportion to distance from the origin. Feet read as metres scale everything by 1 ÷ 0.3048 = 3.28. Test: compare a known length in both layers; correct by rescaling.

Cause 4, georeferencing and digitising error. Offsets are small and irregular, a few metres in different directions. Test: inspect the control-point residuals and RMS (for example 2.24 m against a 5 m tolerance); correct by adding or replacing control points and refitting.

Cause 5, different source scales. A 1:50 000 layer (allowed 12.5 m) against a 1:4000 layer (allowed 1.0 m) will disagree by up to about 12 m even when both are correct. Test: read the source scale in metadata; correct by using the larger-scale source for boundaries.

Cause 6, generalisation and slivers. Shared boundaries digitised separately leave thin slivers after overlay. Test: count sliver polygons below a width threshold; correct by snapping to one master boundary and cleaning topology.
Order of repair: datum, then projection, then units, then georeferencing, then slivers, and recheck the offsets at the same features after each step. Record what was done in metadata.

Independent test: display both layers over a current satellite image in the common system. The layer that matches the image at the control features is taken as correct, and only the other layer is repaired, so a good layer is never moved to fit a bad one.
Check. √(152² + 214²) = √(23 104 + 45 796) = √68 900 = 262.5 m; 12.5 − 1.0 = 11.5 m allowed disagreement between the two scales.

bank.q: Evaluate the reliability of a GIS-based planning model for rural educational facilities when the population data is a decade old.
outline: Model depends on settlement location and population attributes
Old census understates new growth and migration
Buffers assume uniform travel, ignoring terrain, rivers and bus routes
Scale of source data limits the smallest mappable unit
Positional error in settlement points shifts buffer results
Effects: false gaps reported and schools mis-sited
Mitigations: update with field survey or satellite-derived settlement maps, use road-network travel time instead of straight-line buffers, show sensitivity by rerunning with low and high population
Conclusion: useful for ranking, not for a final site decision

answer.text: What the model uses: habitation points with child population, existing school buffers (for example 5 km), roads, and constraints; the output ranks unserved habitations and candidate sites.

Effect of decade-old data, with numbers. At 1.5 % growth a year, a population grows by 1.015¹⁰ = 1.161, that is 16 %, in ten years. A habitation recorded with 280 children now has about 280 × 1.161 = 325. If the rule needs 300 children to justify a school, the old data wrongly rejects it.
Growth is uneven: villages near towns and highways grow faster, remote ones may shrink by migration, so a single correction factor does not fix the ranking.
Buffers assume straight-line travel. Across a river or hills the road distance can be 1.4 times the straight line, so a habitation 5 km away as the crow flies may be 7 km by road and truly unserved.

Positional and scale error: habitation points digitised from 1:50 000 sheets may be 12.5 m or more off, which matters only near buffer edges; settlements that grew since the survey may be missing as points altogether.
Consequences: false gaps (schools proposed where children have moved away) and missed gaps (new colonies left out), and a ranking that looks precise but is not.

Mitigations: update population from recent household surveys or school enrolment records; map new settlements from current satellite imagery; replace straight-line buffers by network travel distance or time; run the model with low and high growth (for example 1.0 % and 2.0 % a year: 1.105 and 1.219) and keep only sites that rank high in both.
Evaluation: with old data the model is reliable for a first ranking and for showing where to look, not for the final siting decision, which needs a field check of children, access and land.

Sensitivity with numbers: at 1.0 % a year the 280 children become 280 × 1.105 = 309, and at 2.0 % they become 280 × 1.219 = 341, so the habitation clears 300 in both cases and is a robust candidate. One recorded with 260 children gives 287 and 317, clearing 300 only in the high case, so it needs a field count before it is ranked.

bank.q: A building-attribute dataset extracted from imagery has clean geometry but wrong heights and use codes. Discuss the consequences and the verification plan you would enforce.
outline: Distinguish positional accuracy from attribute accuracy
Clean geometry gives false confidence; property tax and planning decisions go wrong
Sources: imagery date, shadow, occlusion, classifier error, manual entry
Error propagation into overlay results, no warning visible to the user
Verification plan: stratified random sample, field check, confusion matrix for classes
Height check against total station or LiDAR sample
Record accuracy in metadata, set acceptance thresholds, rework failing classes
Repeat verification at intervals

answer.text: Two kinds of accuracy. Positional accuracy (is the footprint in the right place and shape?) is good here; attribute accuracy (are the height and use code right?) is poor. A clean geometry makes the wrong attributes look trustworthy.

Consequences: property tax based on floor area, which depends on the number of floors from the height, is wrong; planning checks on building height and land use (for example commercial use in a residential zone) flag the wrong buildings; flood and earthquake exposure counts are off. The overlay shows no warning, so the error passes into every product.
Sources of error: imagery date (new floors added since), shadow and lean in oblique views, trees hiding roofs, classifier confusion between similar roofs, and manual entry slips.
Verification plan, step 1: a stratified random sample, for example 200 of 5000 buildings, spread over wards and building types so that every stratum is tested.

Step 2, use codes: visit the sampled buildings and build an error matrix of code mapped against code found. If 172 of 200 are right, attribute accuracy is 86 %; report per-class user's and producer's accuracy, not just the total.

Step 3, heights: compare with total station or LiDAR heights at the sampled buildings and report RMSE. Differences of +1.2, −0.8, +2.5, −1.5 and +0.6 m give RMSE = √((1.44 + 0.64 + 6.25 + 2.25 + 0.36) ÷ 5) = √2.19 = 1.48 m; a storey is about 3 m, so errors above 1.5 m risk a wrong floor count.
Step 4, acceptance and rework: set thresholds before checking (for example 90 % for use codes and 1.5 m RMSE for heights); classes or wards that fail are re-extracted and checked again.
Step 5, metadata and repetition: record the method, sample, accuracies and image date in the layer's metadata, and repeat the check at each update.

Size of the consequence: a building recorded at 6 m (2 floors) but actually 9 m (3 floors), with a 120 m² footprint, is taxed on 120 × 2 = 240 m² instead of 120 × 3 = 360 m², so a third of its floor area is missed. Repeated across a ward, such errors add up to a large shortfall that the clean map does not reveal.

bank.q: GIS is often described as a decision-support tool rather than a map-making tool. Evaluate this statement using one disaster-management application and one infrastructure-planning application.
outline: Distinguish map output from question answering
Disaster: flood or drought layers combined to rank villages and route relief, decisions change with the model
Infrastructure: corridor selection by overlay of terrain, land cost, settlements and environment
Value lies in combining layers and testing scenarios quickly
Limits: output quality equals input quality, weights are judgement, uncertainty is often hidden
Cost-benefit: saves repeated field visits and reveals conflicts early
Conclusion: decision support when data quality and assumptions are stated, else decorative mapping

answer.text: The claim: a map shows, a decision-support tool answers a question by combining layers, testing scenarios and ranking options. GIS earns the second description when its layers and rules are stated.

Disaster case, flood relief. Layers: river (line), DEM (raster), villages (points with population), roads. Query: villages within 1 km of the river and below 10 m elevation. A 1 km buffer on each side of a 40 km reach covers 2 × 1 × 40 = 80 km² plus the rounded ends (π × 1² = 3.1 km²), 83.1 km². Suppose 18 villages fall inside and 11 of them below 10 m: those 11 are ranked by population for evacuation, and the road layer routes relief around flooded links.
Scenario testing: raise the flood level to 12 m and rerun; the list changes in minutes, which no paper map allows.

Infrastructure case, road corridor. Reclassify terrain slope, land cost, settlements and forest to cost scores 1–5 and combine with weights, for example 0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2. A cell with scores 2, 4, 1, 5 costs 0.6 + 1.2 + 0.2 + 1.0 = 3.0. A least-cost path across the cost surface gives the corridor; changing the forest weight shows how sensitive the alignment is.

Where the value lies: layers combined through location, rules applied the same way everywhere, quick reruns, and conflicts (a corridor through a protected forest, a relief route over a breached bridge) found before field work.

Limits: the output is no better than the inputs (an old DEM or census misleads); weights are judgement and can steer the answer; uncertainty is usually invisible on a clean map; a GIS cannot weigh social and legal issues it holds no layer for.
Cost and benefit: one GIS run replaces many field visits for screening, but the short list still needs a field check.

Evaluation: the statement is true when the data quality, the weights and the assumptions are stated with the map, and the model is used to compare options; without them the same software produces decorative maps that only look like decisions.

glossary.def: An organised system of hardware, software, data, people and methods for capturing, storing, analysing and displaying spatially referenced data.
Global Navigation Satellite System, the family of satellite positioning systems that includes GPS, giving position on a datum such as WGS84.
Assigning real-world coordinates to a scanned map, image or drawing so that it can sit correctly with other layers.
A point with known coordinates, measured by total station or GNSS, used to georeference or to check imagery.
The smallest feature a dataset can show, expressed as raster cell size in metres or as map scale.
The ground size represented by one image pixel in a UAV or aerial photograph, usually given in centimetres.
Converting vector features to a grid of cells, with attribute value assigned to every cell.
Converting a raster or scanned map into points, lines and polygons.
The set of rules that record how features connect and share boundaries, e.g. adjacent polygons share one edge, not two.
A thin false polygon created when two boundary lines that should coincide do not; its strip belongs to neither neighbour.
A table of rows (features) and columns (attributes) linked to geometry by a key field.
A column whose value is unique and is used to join an attribute table to a geometry table.
Data about data: source, date, datum, projection, units, scale and accuracy of a layer.
Combining layers of the same area to obtain a new layer carrying the attributes of the inputs.
A question answered by testing geometry, e.g. list the plots within 100 m of a canal or the wells inside ward 7.
How close a measured value is to the true value, stated as a number in metres or as a class error rate.
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other, independent of accuracy.
The way input errors combine and grow through successive analysis steps so the output is less reliable than any single input.
Digital Elevation Model, a raster of ground elevation values used for slope, contour and volume work.
A geometrically corrected image mosaic in which every pixel is placed at its true map position.
A photogrammetric method that reconstructs camera positions and a 3D surface from many overlapping images.
Computing statistics of one layer within the zones of another, e.g. mean rainfall per watershed.
A polygon at a fixed distance from a feature, used for proximity queries and protected margins.
One thematic set of spatial data, such as roads, within a GIS project.
